label: t2-patterns-lay
topic: Track 2 plain-language explanation: the chemotactic range-expansion front of E. coli in soft agar (Cremer 2019 data, Narla 2021 travelling-wave law), checked against law set 1.8.1
summary:
PLAIN-LANGUAGE PACK FOR TRACK 2. Bracketed tags like [F6] point to the numbered findings in this file (claim text begins with the same tag). Reading level about 9th grade.

A. WHAT ARE WE DOING AND WHY (one paragraph). Some bacteria spread across a dish as a moving ring that can run several times faster than ordinary spreading [F1][F2][F7]. Two published papers describe this ring with data and with a formula [F8][F9][F10]. We are using it as a test case for a bigger question: when a scientist writes down a rule for how a living pattern forms, can the rule be checked honestly against measurements that were not used to build it? We will first write down what the rule predicts and only then open the measurements, so nobody (including us) can quietly adjust the rule afterwards [F22]. The aim is not a new discovery about bacteria. It is a fair, repeatable check of a named rule, and an honest record of where it holds and where it breaks [F12][F13].

B. HOW, STEP BY STEP (each step has an everyday comparison).
1. Pick the system. We study the common gut bacterium E. coli spreading from a spot in a dish of soft agar, a jelly so loose that cells can swim through it [F3]. Comparison: a drop of ink spreading in a thin gel, except the ink is alive and steers.
2. Name what we measure. The first number is how fast the outer edge of the colony moves outward, in millimetres per hour; the second is how fast the cells double, in doublings-rate per hour [F6]. Comparison: the speed of a spreading crowd and how quickly the crowd is having babies.
3. Understand the effect being explained. When the jelly holds a little attractant (a food-like smell), the cells form a travelling ring at the edge and move much faster than cells that only wander and multiply [F1][F2][F4][F7]. Comparison: a crowd that follows a smell trail it is itself laying down, instead of wandering at random.
4. Write down the formula. One paper gives a formula in which the edge speed grows with the square root of the growth rate and with the square root of how strong the attractant is compared with the weakest level the cells can sense, and does not depend on how fast cells eat the attractant [F8][F9][F10]. Comparison: a recipe card that says which dials matter and which do not.
5. Set the simple baseline. We fit one number to six ordinary-cell measurements, so that speed squared is a fixed multiple of growth rate [F12]. Comparison: a rule of thumb that has no biology in it, used as the bar to beat.
6. Write predictions before opening new data. The earlier design lists six predictions with pass and fail lines, kept in a dated file that is not edited afterwards [F22]. Comparison: sealing your guess in an envelope before the race.
7. Open the held-out measurements. These are cells with modified food uptake, a mixture of two attractants, and measurements of single swimming cells, none of which were used to set the formula [F22]. Comparison: the exam questions you did not see while studying.
8. Score each prediction as passed, failed or inconclusive. A failure is kept and reported, never removed [F22]. Comparison: a referee who writes down every foul.
9. Check the formula against the law library. The project's law library (version 1.8.1) holds a related candidate law about the minimum speed of a spreading wave, and nothing about chemotactic waves [F17][F18]. Comparison: asking whether a building code already covers the thing we are building.
10. Report the map of what held and what did not. The result is a list of which dependencies in the formula survived the checks, with the conditions under which each holds [F22]. Comparison: a road map with the closed roads marked.

C. WHAT WOULD COUNT AS BEING WRONG (plain words). The design proposes these tests; none has been run yet [F22]. (1) If the formula is right that speed does not depend on how fast cells eat the attractant, strains that eat it at different rates should front at about the same speed; a clear trend would show it is wrong. (2) The formula says the density of cells in the ring should go down in proportion to how fast they eat the attractant, so a strain that eats about three times slower should have about three times denser rings; if the density does not follow within the stated range, the formula is wrong there. (3) The formula says the cell density behind the ring rises smoothly with a length equal to speed divided by growth rate; a measured length more than 30 percent off would count as wrong. (4) If the single-cell swimming data cannot explain why speed rises faster than the square root of growth rate in the food-uptake series, that explanation is dropped. Already seen, so not blind: the square-root-of-growth rule is already known to miss many modified strains [F13][F14], and the dependence on attractant strength is already known to look weaker than square-root in the seen data (design-patterns.json, own calculation).

D. WHAT COULD GO WRONG. (1) Our guess can be partly leaked: the published figures show the data we call unseen, so only the numeric files are unopened [design-patterns.json risks]. (2) The formula was copied from a computer-readable version of the paper by an earlier agent and must be checked against the PDF before any freeze [design-patterns.json risks]. (3) Some conditions have only one or two repeats, so averages are shaky [F6 table]. (4) The standard chemotaxis model can fail at high cell density, which the formula may inherit [F16]. (5) The jelly dish is not a gut or soil, so the result says little about wild settings by itself. (6) The related library law is a candidate, not accepted, and only proves arithmetic about a formula, not that a colony obeys it [F17]. (7) We have no wet lab here, so nothing new is grown; 'new' means new to our fit.

E. GLOSSARY: see the glossary field (ten terms).

F. THREE QUESTIONS A LAYPERSON WOULD ASK.
Q1. Why does a formula for a bacteria ring matter? Honest answer: on its own, little outside this system. It matters here as a clean test of whether a rule, checked on conditions it was not built from, keeps working. Where it breaks is as informative as where it holds [F12][F13].
Q2. Is this proving that bacteria smell their way across a dish? Honest answer: that finding comes from the Cremer paper, which reports that chemotaxis in food-rich conditions speeds up expansion [F1][F2]. Our work does not re-prove it. We test whether a formula for the speed holds up.
Q3. If the simple rule already fits the normal cells, why bother with the rest? Honest answer: because it fits only six measurements, then misses most of the other seventeen we checked, by 8 to 94 percent [F12][F13]. A rule that works only where it was tuned is not yet a law.
lay_summary: Imagine a drop of living ink spreading in a dish of clear jelly. Bacteria called E. coli do not just drift outward. They follow a faint smell of food that they themselves use up, and this makes a ring at the edge that moves several times faster than plain wandering [F1][F2][F7]. Scientists have a formula for how fast the ring should move [F8][F9][F10]. We are checking that formula on measurements it was not tuned on, and we write down our predictions first so we cannot cheat. A very simple rule fits six normal measurements within about 11 percent but misses most of the others, so the formula still has to prove itself [F12][F13].

findings.claim: [F1] In a Cremer et al. 2019 Nature paper, chemotaxis (directed movement along chemical gradients) in nutrient-rich conditions makes E. coli populations expand into empty territory.
findings.evidence_quote: Chemotaxis in nutrient-replete conditions promotes the expansion of bacterial populations into unoccupied territories well before nutrients run out in the current environment.

findings.claim: [F2] Low attractant levels act as 'aroma-like cues' that set the direction and raise the speed of population movement along self-generated attractant gradients; this is faster than unguided Fisher-Kolmogorov expansion.
findings.evidence_quote: Low levels of chemoattractants act as aroma-like cues in this process, establishing the direction and enhancing the speed of population movement along the self-generated attractant gradients.

findings.claim: [F3] Expansion speeds were measured on soft-agar plates containing 0.25 percent agar.
findings.evidence_quote: Expansion speeds were measured using soft-agar plates containing 0.25% agar and growth media resembled to the liquid culture conditions introduced above.

findings.claim: [F4] The moving ring shows up as a bulge in the cell-density profile just behind a steep exponential rise at the front.
findings.evidence_quote: The chemotactic ring is seen as a bulge in the density profile following the steep (exponential) increase at the front

findings.claim: [F5] In one example (glycerol as food, a low amount of aspartate as attractant) the front bulge advanced at about 3.2 mm per hour, followed by a broad exponentially increasing density behind it.
findings.evidence_quote: Strikingly, the advance of the front bulge (~3.2 mm / h ) is steadily followed by a trailing region with a broad, exponentially increasing density profile

findings.claim: [F6] Wild-type E. coli (strain HE206) on 20 mM glucose with 100 uM aspartate in 0.25 percent agar: mean expansion speed 4.335 mm/h (n=5) and growth rate 0.9985 per hour; on 40 mM glycerol: 3.675 mm/h and 0.7735 per hour.

findings.claim: [F7] Without chemotaxis the Fisher speed 2*sqrt(D*r), computed with the simulation file's cell diffusion coefficient 50.2e-12 m^2/s (0.18072 mm^2/h), would be 0.850 mm/h (glucose) and 0.748 mm/h (glycerol); the measured chemotactic front is 5.10 and 4.91 times faster. This is illustrative: D is the model's value, not a separately measured one.
findings.source: Own calculation: python -E -P scripts/t2-patterns-lay/calc2.py MOESM11.xlsx (arithmetic: D=50.2e-12*3.6e9=0.18072 mm^2/h; c_F=2*sqrt(0.18072*0.9985)=0.850; 4.3347/0.850=5.10). D from MOESM3.txt line 31 'D_chemotaxis_1: 50.2e-12' (sha256 40072304946f8e5ff32ec7dfcbcd5efba11b97bdb54dda0dd0a6214df0f78d38). Fisher speed formula named in PMC8640786.
findings.evidence_quote: it is not sufficient to explain the high expansion speeds of the bacterial front observed in populations of chemotactic bacteria

findings.claim: [F8] Narla, Cremer and Hwa (2021) report that the front speed of the growth-expansion model depends on the square root of the growth rate.
findings.evidence_quote: First, there is a square root dependence on the growth rate r , as validated by numerical results in Fig. 2 A .

findings.claim: [F9] The same paper reports that speed increases with the square root of the relative background attractant concentration a0/am.
findings.evidence_quote: The expansion speed is further increased by the square root of the relative background attractant concentration, a 0 / a m ( Fig. 2 B ).

findings.claim: [F10] The same paper reports that speed does not depend on the attractant uptake rate or on the starting population size.
findings.value: no dependence on uptake rate mu
findings.evidence_quote: However, the expansion speed c does not depend on the specific rate of attractant uptake μ ( Fig. 2 C ) nor the inoculum population size

findings.claim: [F11] The paper's abstract says speeds can be boosted by orders of magnitude when the environment's chemical availability is high relative to the cells' sensing limits.
findings.evidence_quote: expansion speeds can be boosted by orders of magnitude when the environmental availability of chemicals relative to the cellular limits of chemical sensing is high.

findings.claim: [F12] A one-number baseline u^2 = k*r (least squares through the origin) fitted on the six wild-type aspartate rows gives k = 16.904 mm^2/h and reproduces those six rows within -9.6 to +11.1 percent. (An earlier agent reported 16.907; the difference is rounding in the fit.)
findings.source: Own calculation, scripts/t2-patterns-lay/calc2.py on MOESM11.xlsx rows 3-8; output scratch/t2-patterns-lay/calc2.out. Arithmetic: k = sum(u^2 r)/sum(r^2).

findings.claim: [F13] On the 17 other rows with aspartate or serine (modified strains, serine rows, no-inducer rows) this baseline is off by 7.8 to 94.0 percent and only 7 of 17 are within 15 percent. This is a crude no-mechanism control, not the authors' full model, whose parameters vary with growth condition.
findings.source: Own calculation, scripts/t2-patterns-lay/calc2.py, output scratch/t2-patterns-lay/calc2.out ('n heldout 17 min|err| 7.8 max|err| 94.0 ... n within 15%: 7'). The full-model remark: PMC6883170 text 'The full model, including the observed growth-rate dependencies of the macroscopic parameters ... describes the observed data very well'.

findings.claim: [F14] In the glycerol-uptake titration strain HE443 (aspartate), growth rate rose from 0.222 to 0.738 per hour (x3.32) while front speed rose from 0.999 to 4.171 mm/h (x4.18); a square-root law would predict only x1.82 (sqrt 3.32).
findings.source: Own calculation from MOESM11.xlsx HE443 rows with 0 and 800 uM inducer: 0.738211488/0.222=3.325; 4.170896515/0.9986998405=4.176; sqrt(3.325)=1.82.
findings.value: speed x4.18 vs growth x3.32; sqrt-law x1.82

findings.claim: [F15] Swimming speed of the E. coli strains stayed high through steady exponential growth and fell on starvation, so cells keep swimming while growing.
findings.evidence_quote: the swimming speed actually remained high throughout steady exponential growth, but declined rapidly upon entering starvation in both minimal and rich media

findings.claim: [F16] Phan et al. 2024 (PNAS) report that the standard Patlak-Keller-Segel model of collective chemotactic migration breaks down at high cell densities, using a fluorescent aspartate sensor. The abstract does not say whether the setup was soft agar, so how far it applies to this track is not established.
findings.evidence_quote: Our measurements show that the standard Patlak-Keller-Segel model for collective chemotactic bacterial migration breaks down at high cell densities.

findings.claim: [F17] Law set 1.8.1 contains fisher-kpp-speed 1.1.0 with status candidate (non-binding). Its statement is that c^2 = 4*s*D gives the minimum of the family of linear spreading speeds; its checkable direction is a lower bound, and its scope excludes showing that a travelling wave exists or that any population disperses diffusively.
findings.evidence_quote: so c is the minimum of the family of linear spreading speeds and is attained at exactly one decay rate

findings.claim: [F18] I found no law in the registry about chemotaxis or Keller-Segel waves: a text search of registry/laws and registry/lawsets for 'chemotax' and 'Keller' returned nothing. The only other pattern law, turing-ddi 1.1.0 (two-species reaction-diffusion), is also candidate and does not describe this single-population front.
findings.source: Own search: grep -rn 'chemotax\|Keller' in lean/registry/laws and lean/registry/lawsets (no hits); lawsets/lawset-1.8.1.json for turing-ddi status
findings.evidence_quote: the four genuine discovery candidates (turing-ddi, kimura-heterozygosity, maynardsmith-hawk-dove, fisher-kpp-speed) stay candidate and stay non-binding.

findings.claim: [F19] Correction to the earlier law-mapper: laws-patterns.json and design-patterns.json were written against law set 1.6.0 and say the library has no travelling-front law. Law set 1.8.1 does list fisher-kpp-speed (introduced in 1.8.0), as a candidate.
findings.evidence_quote: "introduced_in": "1.8.0",

findings.claim: [F20] Fisher's 1937 paper 'The wave of advance of advantageous genes', the source of the Fisher-KPP idea cited by the library law, resolves in Crossref.
findings.evidence_quote: THE WAVE OF ADVANCE OF ADVANTAGEOUS GENES

findings.claim: [F21] Raw confocal density scans of expanding populations exist as a public dataset 'Confocal intensity scans expanding bacteria' (2019, CC BY 4.0). Its 168,455,158-byte size is from the earlier design agent's figshare API fetch; I confirmed title and licence only.
findings.evidence_quote: Confocal intensity scans expanding bacteria

findings.claim: [F22] The earlier design proposes six predictions (F1 to F6 in that file) with refutation thresholds, to be recorded before the unopened data are read. They had not been run at the time that file was written, and I did not find or verify a commit that freezes them.
findings.evidence_quote: Six predictions are frozen in one git commit before any data module for those sheets exists.

key_claims.claim: Chemotaxis along attractant gradients the cells make themselves lets an E. coli population expand faster than unguided growth-plus-wandering (Cremer 2019).
key_claims.evidence_quote: Low levels of chemoattractants act as aroma-like cues in this process, establishing the direction and enhancing the speed of population movement along the self-generated attractant gradients.

key_claims.claim: Narla 2021 states the formula's dependences: speed grows with the square root of growth rate and of relative attractant level, and does not depend on uptake rate.
key_claims.evidence_quote: First, there is a square root dependence on the growth rate r , as validated by numerical results in Fig. 2 A .

key_claims.claim: A square-root-of-growth baseline fitted on six wild-type rows (k = 16.904 mm^2/h) misses most of the other 17 conditions (only 7 within 15 percent; errors 7.8 to 94.0 percent). This is my own calculation and uses a crude control, not the authors' full model.
Law set 1.8.1 has no chemotaxis law; its only related law, fisher-kpp-speed 1.1.0, is a candidate and non-binding.

glossary.plain: A common bacterium that lives in animal guts and is easy to grow in a lab.
A jelly so loose (0.25 percent agar here) that cells can swim through it instead of sitting on top.
A cell steering toward or away from a chemical, the way you follow the smell of baking bread.
A chemical that cells are drawn toward; here, the amino acid aspartate or serine.
How fast the cells multiply, measured in doublings per hour in a liquid flask.
How fast the outer edge of the spreading colony moves, in millimetres per hour.
A pattern that keeps its shape while moving, like a stadium wave.
The speed of a front when cells only wander at random and multiply, with no steering.
Measurements kept out of the fitting so they can test the rule fairly.
A rule the project has written and machine-checked but not yet accepted, so it cannot reject a design on its own.

recommendations: Before this explanation is shown to anyone, re-check the square-root dependences against the Narla PDF and the SI appendix; I quoted the text of the Europe PMC version only.
State in any public text that the 'not yet seen' data are only numerically unopened, since the paper figures show them [F22].
Rerun the whole check against law set 1.8.1 and add fisher-kpp-speed as a candidate cross-check, not as proof [F17][F19].
Read Phan 2024 in full to see whether its setup matches soft agar before relying on it for the density caveat [F16].

could_not_find: I did not download any new dataset; the 168 MB confocal archive was not fetched (over the 20 MB per-download limit), so profile shapes (the bulge, the exponential tail) are described from text only, and no density numbers are given.
I did not read the Narla SI appendix or the PDF; the formula's exact form was not re-derived here, only its stated dependences from the main text.
I could not confirm that the six proposed predictions were committed to a dated file; I found no such commit in this run [F22].
I did not find a second laboratory's public front-speed dataset for the same system.
Phan 2024 was read by abstract only; whether its setup resembles soft agar is not established [F16].
The Lean statement for fisher-kpp-speed was not built or re-run (no Lean run was needed; reading the registry JSON was enough). Its proof status beyond the registry record is unverified by me.
The 'unverified background' idea that cells in a gut or soil behave like this was deliberately not claimed; no source was fetched for it.
Free C: disk was 5.6 GB and D: 9.5 GB, above the thresholds, so no heavy command was blocked; none was needed.
